1:
The psalm's superscription sets the witnesses a puzzle before a word of prayer is heard. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry observes that the title has nothing peculiar in it save that it is said to be upon Nehiloth, "a word nowhere else used," and offers what he owns is "but a conjecture" — that it signifies wind-instruments, as Neginoth was thought to mean the stringed. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke presses the same etymology, taking nechiloth from a root "to be hollow, to bore through," and so of any wind-instrument, the horn, trumpet, or flute; yet he records too the Septuagint's very different rendering, "In favour of her who obtains the inheritance," which derived the word from nachal, to inherit, and referred it either to Israel's inheritance of the promised land or to the Church that inherits through Christ.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch deny that the inscription is a motto of the contents at all: whatever is joined to "to the chief Musician" bears on the music, and nechiloth, if from nachal, might rather mean "swarms" — swarms of bees — naming a popular melody, a tune resembling, as Hai Gaon fancied, the hum of bees. The reformed John Calvin refuses to treat these titles "as if they were riddles," and rests content that it was some instrument or tune, "of what particular kind I consider it of little importance to ascertain." Behind the philology the latin-fathers Augustine hears the whole psalm as the voice of the Church, called to her inheritance that she may herself become the inheritance of the Lord.

With the title behind them the witnesses take up the first petition. The reformed John Gill reads "give ear to my words" of vocal prayer, the words a man freely utters at the throne of grace under the Spirit's direction, distinguished from the silent "meditation of the heart" — the holy boldness, the parrhesia, that the saints are allowed before God. On that "meditation" Charles Ellicott, also grammatical-historical, notes a word cognate with the "meditate" of Ps. 1:2, meaning to mutter or murmur, a "whispered prayer" set between the spoken "words" and the loud "voice of my cry." Calvin hears in it the "dove-like mournings" of Bishop Horne and the "sighing" of Horsley, a confused muttering like Hezekiah's chattering "like a crane or a swallow" in Isa. 38:14. The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon gathers them: there are two sorts of prayer, the words and the "unuttered longings," for "words are not the essence but the garments of prayer," as Moses cried at the Red Sea though he said nothing.
2:
The plea grows more intimate as David names the God he prays to. The reformed John Gill hears in "the voice of my cry" something more than groans or words, a loud outcry of a soul in great distress, and marks the first of the arguments David presses — his own interest in, and relation to, the Lord. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lingers on the styling: to call God "my King and my God" is the most commanding principle of prayer and the most prevailing plea in it, for kings on their own thrones — as David was — must yet be beggars at God's throne, owning peculiar obligations and expecting peculiar help.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch turn to the Hebrew of the surrounding lines, where the verbal adjective for one who has "pleasure" in a thing takes the accusative, and the verb "to dwell" or "sojourn" governs its object directly, so that evil, conceived as a person, cannot so much as lodge with a holy God. Their interest is grammatical, but it serves the prayer: the God addressed as King is the God with whom wickedness can find no abode.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke traces the very movement of David's waking soul — how, remembering the goodness of God on which he had lain down to sleep, he feels his need of continual protection, forms his meditation into words, and, accustomed to answered prayer, grows importunate and lifts up his voice. Clarke preserves a pretty turn from Rabbi Jarchi that catches the two registers of the psalm: "When I have power to pray, and to ask for the things I need, then, O Lord, give ear to my words; but when I have no power to plead with thee, and fear seizes on my heart, then, O Lord, consider my meditation." The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon fastens on "these little pronouns, my King, and my God," as "the pith and marrow of the plea": we are not aliens but subjects, not strangers but worshippers, ours "by covenant, by promise, by oath, by blood," and a king is expected to hear the appeals of his own people. He hears, too, the eloquence of a mere cry: as in another psalm David spoke of "the voice of my weeping," so weeping and crying have a voice of their own that reaches the very heart of God, for "to a loving father his children's cries are music." And on "unto thee will I pray" Spurgeon finds a resolution as much as a request, David vowing that as long as he lived he would never cease to supplicate, though the answer tarried.
3:
Morning is the hour David fixes for his approach, and the witnesses dwell both on the time and on the archer's image that follows. The reformed John Gill takes "my voice shalt thou hear in the morning" both as confidence that God will hear early, quickly, and seasonably, and as a resolve to seek God first of all: the morning is the proper season to return thanks for rest and to ask keeping for the day, and God should be sought in the first place. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, reading the psalm as a morning hymn answering the evening hymn before it, finds it good "to begin the day with God," since what first occupies the mind on waking is likeliest to keep the heart all day; and he catches the metaphor of the archer in "I will direct my prayer" — David sees his mark, sets the arrow to the bow, takes his aim, lets fly, and then "looks up" to see whether he has hit.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the same verb another way. "Direct," he says, is better "prepare," the very word used of the priest laying the wood in order upon the altar or setting out the parts of the sacrifice, so that David arranges his prayer as a morning offering — a hint, Ellicott thinks, that the author may himself have been a priest, and that "offering," not "prayer," is the word to be supplied. And "look up," he adds, is from the root that gives Mizpeh, a watch-tower: the psalmist looks up for his answer as the seer on his tower in Hab. 2:1 looked up for his vision, an attitude of raised eyes less usual in the East than standing or prostrate prayer.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads "in the morning" simply: "every morning; as soon as I wake, I am still with thee … the first thing that I do is to pray to thee." The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon binds the two images together and presses the resolve in them — "this is not so much a prayer as a resolution": David will not be dumb, for "we can sooner die than live without prayer," and morning is the fittest hour, when "an hour in the morning is worth two in the evening" and grace may drop upon the soul while the dew is yet on the grass. Prayer, Spurgeon says, should be "the key of the day and the lock of the night." The witnesses converge: the morning voice is aimed like an arrow and laid out like a sacrifice, and then the eye is lifted to watch for its return.
4:
"For thou art not a God that hath pleasure in wickedness" — the prayer now grounds itself in the very nature of the God addressed, and the witnesses read the line as David's argument against his enemies drawn from God's holiness. The reformed John Gill insists the words touch God's nature and will: sin is "the abominable thing which his righteous soul hates," so contrary to his purity that he takes no pleasure in it — though Gill is careful to add that this hatred of the sin is not inconsistent with God's delight in the persons of his elect in Christ, in whom he loves them while yet they are sinners in themselves.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the line under the head of "a sin-hating God," and makes it serve two ends at once — a warning to the praying soul that, though God is ready to hear, "if we regard iniquity in our heart" he will not hear our prayers, as Ps. 66:18 says; and an encouragement against David's enemies, who, as wicked men, are enemies to God and such as he has no pleasure in. When God says he takes no pleasure in wickedness, Henry glosses, he means "thou art a God that hates it," even the wickedness that men cover "with a cloak of religion."

On the second clause the wesleyan-arminian and grammatical-historical voices press the Hebrew. Adam Clarke renders "neither shall evil dwell with thee" more strictly, "the evil man shall not even sojourn with thee" — not so much as lodge a night in God's house. Charles Ellicott renders it to the same effect, "the wicked man is not thy guest," and points for the contrast to God's promise to dwell with the humble and contrite in Isa. 57:15, and to the portrait of the acceptable worshipper in Ps. 15. John Wesley keeps it plain: God does not "approve of, nor delight in" the wicked or their prayers, nor will he have any "fellowship" with them. The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon turns the doctrine into the plea itself: when David prays against his tempters he prays "against the very things which thou thyself abhorrest," and he warns how foolish it is to try to entertain two guests so hostile as Christ and the devil, for "Christ will not live in the parlour of our hearts if we entertain the devil in the cellar of our thoughts."
5:
The catalogue of those God cannot abide opens with "the foolish," and the witnesses agree that the folly meant is moral, not mental. The reformed John Gill explains that these are not the simple but the wicked and ungodly; the word springs from a root meaning "to praise," so that it fits the self-praisers, the proud boasters "elated with their own excellency, with their wisdom, strength, honours, riches, and righteousness," who trust in themselves that they are righteous and despise others — whence the Syriac renders it "the proud" and the Chaldee "mockers." The Septuagint, Gill observes, renders the word "transgressors of the law," the Vulgate "the unrighteous," and the Arabic "they that contradict thy precepts" — all circling the same moral folly. That they "shall not stand in thy sight" denotes, Gill says, God's abhorrence, as a man cannot bear to look on one he detests; they shall receive no favour, however much, like proud Haman, they fancy themselves the king's favourites.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the folly as a kind of madness: he is "a fool and a madman who is running himself out of breath for no prize, who is fighting against the Almighty," and this every wicked man does. And on the next clause he weighs the dreadful reach of the second line — "thou hatest all workers of iniquity" — distinguishing those who sin now and then from those who "labour in it with all their might," and marvelling that even "the God of infinite love and mercy" hates such, whose portion is "the hatred of God Almighty."

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms the sense of the Hebrew, rendering the "foolish" literally as "shiners" — that is, displayers of self, self-praisers, boasters — and glosses "shall not stand" by the picture of distinguished men standing before kings in Prov. 22:29, or of the angels who "stand" in the court of the heavenly King in Job 1:6; the boaster is precisely the man who shall have no such standing before God. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sums the justice of it: "sin is folly, and sinners are the greatest of all fools" — not fools of God's making, whom he pities, but "fools of their own making," and those he hates; wicked people hate God, and justly therefore are they hated of him, to their endless misery and ruin. The witnesses do not divide: the "foolish" is the self-exalting sinner, and his self-display is the very thing that cannot stand in the sight of a holy God.
6:
The indictment sharpens from folly to falsehood and blood. The reformed John Gill takes "them that speak leasing" — that is, a lie — of falsehood whether in religion or in common speech: false doctrines, errors, and heresies are lies, and the followers of the man of sin "speak lies in hypocrisy"; but so too are the everyday lies that make a man like Satan and abominable to God. Such God will destroy, Gill says, whether with bodily disease, as Gehazi with leprosy, or with sudden death, as Ananias and Sapphira, or with the everlasting destruction of body and soul, "for all liars have their part in the lake which burns with fire and brimstone."

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke traces the old word "leasing" through the Anglo-Saxon for a lie or falsity, and reads the second clause of "the man of bloods," for "he who has the spirit of a murderer will rarely end with one bloodshedding" — as, he adds, those who clamoured for the blood of Christ went on to add the blood of his disciples. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott keeps to the wording, noting that "bloody" is literally "of bloods and deceit," as the ancient versions render it, so that violence and treachery are named together in the one man; and he refers the reader back to the same word "leasing" at Ps. 4:2, where lying vanity was first arraigned.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the two sorts of sinner marked here for destruction. There are, first, the false: those "that speak leasing or lying, and that are deceitful," on whom Scripture lays a particular emphasis, for nothing is "more contrary, and therefore nothing more hateful, to the God of truth." And there are, second, the cruel — "thou wilt abhor the bloody man" — for inhumanity is no less contrary, no less hateful, to the God of mercy "whom mercy pleases." Liars and murderers, Henry says, are "in a particular manner said to resemble the devil and to be his children," and it may well be expected that God should abhor them; these were the characters of David's enemies, and such are still the enemies of Christ and his church. The witnesses do not divide: the God who takes no pleasure in wickedness is here shown hating the two sins in which wickedness most nakedly appears — the lie that betrays the God of truth, and the blood that outrages the God of mercy.
7:
Over against the banished workers of iniquity David sets his own resolve, "But as for me, I will come into thy house." The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry notes how the very holiness that drives sinners away draws the upright near: "God's holiness and justice are so far from being a terror to the upright in heart, to drive them from God, that they are rather by them invited to cleave to him." David resolves, Henry says, to worship God, and to worship him publicly in the courts of his house, though he "prayed often alone" — for "the duties of the closet are designed to prepare us for, not to excuse us from, public ordinances" — and to worship reverently, "in thy fear," with the holy awe pressed in Heb. 12:28.

The reformed John Gill fixes the "house" as the tabernacle of Moses, for the temple was not yet built; there David had been used to go, and though now in a kind of exile from it he was confident he should enter it again. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch add that it is "by the greatness and fulness of divine favour" that David has his access to the sanctuary — the tabernacle on Zion where the ark of the covenant stood, and where daily service was kept. On the ground of his coming the witnesses are one. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke marks that it is "in the multitude of thy mercy," not in any merit of his own, that David dares approach — "he who takes David's views of this subject will never willingly be absent from the means of grace" — and that "in thy fear" he will bow and prostrate himself "in the deepest self-abasement and humility." The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley glosses the clauses in turn: to come "with holy boldness," trusting "only in thy great mercy," and worshipping "with an holy dread and reverence of thy majesty."

The one difficulty is the "holy temple" toward which David worships, for the temple did not yet stand. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott insists the words "house … temple" must be taken literally and not, with Hupfeld, spiritually, granting that the psalm-titles were not framed with historical exactness; the worship intended is real bowing toward the sanctuary, as in 1 Kings 8:29. Clarke reconciles the anachronism by taking "temple" of the holy of holies within the tabernacle, or of that heavenly temple where "Jesus was ever the temple where the Supreme Deity was met with and worshipped." The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon reads it the same devout way: the temple was not built on earth, "but David was wont to turn his eyes spiritually to that temple of God's holiness" where Jehovah dwells between the cherubim — "Daniel opened his window towards Jerusalem, but we open our hearts towards heaven."
8:
Even within the sanctuary David knows he needs leading, and prays, "Lead me, O Lord, in thy righteousness because of mine enemies." The reformed John Gill weighs the "righteousness": it is not David's but God's — the righteousness revealed in the Gospel and imputed by God, in which alone a man may stand and worship; or else the way of God's righteous statutes, in which the Lord leads his people; or God's leading "for his righteousness' sake," his faithfulness to his promises. For David "was very sensible that the way of man is not in himself," and could not direct his own steps.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the "enemies" as, literally, "those watching for" or lying in wait, and notes that Aquila and Jerome both give "those lying in ambush"; God's guidance would enable the good man to avoid their snares and walk straight, "for to walk in God's way is to walk in safety." The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the same lesson from the malice of the watchers: the more curiously his enemies spied his faults, the more cautious David was to avoid all appearance of sin, committing himself to a divine guidance that "the most critical and captious of his enemies, like Daniel's, might find no occasion against him" — and he points to the answer of this very prayer in 1 Sam. 18:14, where David behaved himself wisely and the LORD was with him.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke presses that we need God not only "to bring us to his house, but to keep our feet while we are there," and reads "make thy way straight" as a prayer to be shown that he must go right on, with the divine light always on his path; John Wesley glosses "the way" as "the way wherein thou wouldst have me to walk," and "plain" as "that I may clearly discern it, and readily walk in it." The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon gathers the tenderness of the petition: "Lead me, O Lord, as a little child is led by its father, as a blind man is guided by his friend"; and it is "thy righteousness," not mine, "thy way," not my own, that he asks to be led in — "when we have learned to give up our own way, and long to walk in God's way, it is a happy sign of grace." The witnesses do not divide; the man who has just entered God's house asks at once to be kept from stumbling in it, before the watching eyes of those who wait for his fall.
9:
"For there is no faithfulness in their mouth" — the character of the watching enemies is now laid bare, and the witnesses find in the verse the whole anatomy of a corrupt speech. The reformed John Gill hears in it that there is "no steadfastness, nothing right, sure, or firm" in what such men say, nothing to be depended on; and what was true of David's enemies was true of Christ's, and of the enemies of his Gospel — the false teachers who "handle the word of God deceitfully, and speak lies in hypocrisy." They are, he says, "an assembly of treacherous men."

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends closely to the poetry. "Wickedness," he says, is properly "an abyss," from a root "to fall," set in parallel with the "open sepulchre" of the next clause; and the verse is an instance of "introverted parallelism," the outer "mouth" answering to the inner "tongue." The "open sepulchre" is "at once dangerous and noisome," and "they flatter with their tongue" is literally "make smooth the tongue" — the smooth speech of Ps. 12:2, which he likens to Milton's fiend who "dissembled, and this answer smooth returned." The wesleyan-arminian voices keep the image vivid: Adam Clarke reads the throat "continually gaping for the dead," sending forth "effluvia destructive to the living," and fears the verse "too true a picture of the whole human race"; John Wesley calls the throat "wide opened, ready to devour," a metaphor "from wild beasts gaping for the prey."

The puritan-evangelical voices trace the line's reach into the New Testament. Matthew Henry hears the enemies described as deceitful and bloody at once — their inward part "very wickedness," their throat "an open sepulchre, cruel as the grave, gaping to devour," insatiable as the grave that never says "It is enough" in Prov. 30:15-16 — and notes that the whole is quoted in Rom. 3:13 to prove the general corruption of mankind. Charles Spurgeon presses the same apostolic use, that Paul set this "accurate description … not of David's enemies only, but of all men by nature," and draws from the figure a strange comfort: as an open sepulchre spreads death, so the slanderer would "bury your character in the hideous sepulchre of his own wicked throat" — yet at the resurrection "there will be a resurrection not only of bodies, but characters," and the upright shall "shine forth as the sun."
10:
From describing his enemies David turns to praying against them, and the witnesses divide over whether the words are petition or prophecy. The reformed John Gill reads "destroy thou them, O God" as a prayer, and weighs the Hebrew "make them guilty" — that they be made to appear guilty, whether to themselves, that they may confess, or to others, in a sentence of condemnation, as the Chaldee and Syriac render it "condemn them"; so God may "destroy them, soul and body, with an everlasting destruction." The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, by contrast, would soften the imprecation into a forecast: "all these apparently imprecatory declarations should be translated in the future tense … which shows them to be prophetic — Thou wilt destroy them; thou wilt cast them out."

The grammatical-historical witnesses supply the philology. Charles Ellicott too renders "destroy" literally "make or count guilty," and "transgressions" literally "revolts," in close parallel with the next clause; he notes the ancient alternative of the Septuagint and Vulgate, "let them fall from their counsels" — that is, "let their plots fail" — beside the received "let them fall by their own counsels." Keil and Delitzsch dwell on the verb that unites in itself the three allied senses of "becoming guilty," of "a feeling of guilt," and of "expiation," so that the causative asks God to make the enemy render the penance his fault has earned; and they mark that here, amid the Jehovic psalms, God is called Elohim, "perhaps not altogether unintentionally, as being God the Judge."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry holds petition and prophecy together. David prays God to "cast them out of his protection and favour, out of the heritage of the Lord, out of the land of the living," for they have "filled up the measure of their iniquity" and may be "easily made to fall by their own counsels," snared in the mischief they devised for others, as in Ps. 7:15. Yet his prayer, Henry insists, "comes not from a spirit of revenge, but from a spirit of prophecy," and rests at last on the plea "they have rebelled against thee": had they been only David's enemies he could have forgiven them, but they are rebels against God. The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon reads the same clause the same way — "against thee, not against me" — for "God's enemies it is not in our power to forgive," and the psalmist here "speaks as a judge, ex officio … as God's mouth," so that the sentence gives no man leave for private malice. So the debate stands: an imprecation asking God to condemn, or a prophecy declaring that he will — but all agree the ground is rebellion against God, not a wrong done to David.
11:
The psalm swings from the doomed to the delivered, and the tone lifts into joy. The reformed John Gill marks who these glad ones are: "those that put their trust in thee" are they who trust "not in themselves, in their own hearts, in their righteousness, or riches, or strength," but in the name and righteousness and strength of the Lord; let them "rejoice in the salvation of the Lord, and in hope of eternal glory and happiness." The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, consistent with his reading of the earlier verses, takes the words again declaratively and prophetically: not merely "let them rejoice," but "all those who put their trust in thee shall rejoice, shall ever shout for joy."

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott lights on the word "rejoice," from a root whose primary sense is "bright," and points to the kindred image of Prov. 13:9, "the light of the righteous rejoiceth" — the joy of the trusting is a shining thing. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the fulness of the petition: "let them have cause to rejoice and hearts to rejoice; fill them with joy … let them ever shout for joy, with holy joy, and that which terminates in God." They are to "be joyful in thee, in thy favour, in thy salvation, not in any creature," and to rejoice "because thou defendest them" — a defending, Henry suggests, that may allude to "the pillar of cloud and fire," the visible token of God's presence overshadowing Israel.

Henry draws from the verse a rule of intercession, that we learn of David "to pray, not for ourselves only, but for others, for all good people, for all that trust in God and love his name," so that "grace be with all that love Christ in sincerity." The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon carries the joy to its ground and its permanence: "joy is the privilege of the believer," and where the wicked "laugh first and weep ever after," the trusting "weep now, but shall rejoice eternally"; the bliss has "a firm foundation, for, O Lord, we are joyful in thee," the eternal God being himself "the well-spring of our bliss." "We love God, and therefore we delight in him," Spurgeon adds, so that the believer has "music in the house, music in the heart, and music in heaven, for the Lord Jehovah is our strength and our song." The witnesses do not divide; over against the enemies who fall by their own counsels stands a people whose gladness is safe because its object is God, and whose shout of joy is as lasting as the God they trust.
12:
"For thou, Lord, wilt bless the righteous" — the psalm closes on a benediction, and the witnesses gather to define the blessing and the shield that guards it. The reformed John Gill unfolds the blessing from its root: God has blessed the righteous "with a righteousness, even the righteousness of God imputed to him, by which he is denominated righteous, and with the forgiveness of his sins," and will bless him further "with peace and prosperity, with all spiritual blessings … the blessings of grace here, and glory hereafter" — whence he has "just reason to rejoice and be glad." The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks who "the righteous" are: they "put their trust in God" and "love his name," which is "true and pure religion, to live a life of complacency in God and dependence on him"; and those whom God pronounces blessed "are blessed indeed."

On the shield the witnesses press the Hebrew and its history. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott names it tsinnah, "the long large shield fit for a giant," as in 1 Sam. 17:7, which "could protect the whole body"; and he recalls that Luther, asked at Augsburg where he would find shelter if his prince deserted him, answered, "under the shield of heaven." The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads "with favour" as "like a shield, thy favour will crown him," for God's love "is their defence … in all places, times, and circumstances," and bids the reader "keep yourselves in the love of God" of Jude 21; he closes by calling this "the morning's devotion of this excellent man, a model by which every Christian may frame his own."

The puritan-evangelical voices draw out the completeness of the covering. Matthew Henry observes that "a shield, in war, guards only one side, but the favour of God is to the saints a defence on every side," like "the hedge about Job, round about," in Job 1:10, so that while they keep under the divine protection "they are entirely safe and ought to be entirely satisfied." Charles Spurgeon hears in the encircling shield both glory and guard: God's people are "the heirs of blessedness," and the vast ancient shield "as extensive as a man's whole person" surrounds them entirely; with Ainsworth he finds in the word the further idea "of being crowned, so that we wear a royal helmet, which is at once our glory and defence." So the psalm that opened in the fear of a watching enemy ends compassed round with favour — the trusting soul crowned, shielded, and satisfied in the God who blesses the righteous.
